# Finding Love in the Islamic Republic

In Iran, where Islamic law places significant restrictions on the interactions between unmarried men and women, the simple act of finding a romantic partner can prove remarkably difficult. Public displays of affection are prohibited, casual dating is frowned upon, and the traditional venues where young people might meet potential partners in other countries are often closely monitored or entirely off-limits. For many young Iranians, these constraints turn what should be a natural stage of life into a source of frustration and loneliness.

Ahmad, a 27-year-old bachelor, knows this challenge all too well. Like countless others of his generation, he has struggled to find companionship within the boundaries of a society that offers few acceptable pathways to meeting a future spouse. Rather than resign himself to solitude, however, Ahmad and other singles in similar circumstances have found an unexpected solution: they have turned to a cleric.

Jafar Ardabili runs the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, an organization dedicated to helping single Iranians find suitable partners. His method is both practical and carefully structured. Applicants submit photographs and detailed personal profiles, which Ardabili then uses to identify potential matches. Once compatible individuals are found, he arranges supervised meetings, ensuring that the introductions take place within the acceptable religious and social framework of the country. This oversight provides reassurance to families while giving hopeful singles a legitimate opportunity to connect.

What makes Ardabili's work particularly striking is the image of the matchmaker himself. Dressed in the traditional turban and robes of a religious figure, he represents an unusual blend of spiritual authority and modern matchmaking service. It is not the profile one might expect for someone facilitating romance, yet his religious credentials lend his enterprise a legitimacy that resonates within Iranian society.

Ardabili's approach has proven successful since he arranged his very first match a decade ago. Over the years, his institute has helped bring together numerous couples who might otherwise have struggled to find one another. Perhaps most notably, his methods extend a meaningful degree of agency to women, granting them the right to choose their own companions. In a society where women frequently lack such freedom, this element of Ardabili's work stands out as quietly progressive, offering female applicants a voice in one of the most important decisions of their lives.

# In Tehran, a Cleric Plays Cupid Within the Bounds of Faith

*How one religious scholar built a matchmaking practice bridging tradition and the modern search for love*

---

**TEHRAN, Iran** — On a quiet street in the northern part of Iran's capital, past a courtyard shaded by pomegranate trees, Hojjat al-Islam Mehdi Rahmani keeps an office that looks more like a therapist's sitting room than a religious chamber. Two facing sofas. A pot of tea always warm. A shelf lined with worn volumes of jurisprudence beside a laptop displaying spreadsheets of names.

Here, the 54-year-old cleric conducts what he calls "the most sacred work a person can do" — helping strangers find someone to marry.

"People come to me because they are lonely, and because they are searching," Rahmani said, adjusting the folds of his brown robe. "The Quran says God created spouses so that you may find tranquility. My job is to help that tranquility begin."

## A Modern Problem, A Traditional Answer

Iran, like much of the world, is grappling with a marriage crisis. Government figures have shown marriage rates declining for years while the average age of first marriage has climbed, driven by economic pressures, high unemployment among young people, and shifting social expectations.

For a generation of Iranians navigating this landscape, the traditional pathways to marriage — arrangements brokered by families, introductions through relatives — no longer feel sufficient. Dating apps exist but occupy a legal and cultural gray zone. Public courtship remains constrained.

Into this gap step figures like Rahmani, who blend the authority of religious credentials with the practical services of a matchmaker.

"The old way was your mother knew someone's mother," said Zahra, a 31-year-old accountant who asked that only her first name be used. She came to Rahmani after two years of unsuccessful searching. "But families are smaller now. People move to the city alone. Someone like him fills a role that used to belong to a whole village."

## How It Works

Rahmani's process is methodical. New clients complete a lengthy questionnaire covering not only the expected details — age, education, profession — but questions about religious observance, family expectations, and what he calls "the shape of a person's faith."

"Some are very devout, some less so," he explained. "A pious man and a woman who prays rarely — this can work, or it can be a source of pain. I must understand honestly where each person stands."

Meetings between potential matches are chaperoned and take place in his office or in family settings, in accordance with Islamic norms that prohibit unmarried men and women from being alone together. Conversations are encouraged; physical contact is not.

Rahmani sees this structure not as a limitation but as a feature.

"In the West, I am told, people spend years together and still do not truly know each other," he said. "Here, we ask the serious questions early. Do you want children? How will you handle money? Where does God fit in your home? These matter more than a candlelit dinner."

## Between Devotion and Doubt

Not everyone embraces the model. Critics argue that religiously structured matchmaking can reinforce conservative gender expectations, and that the emphasis on family approval can pressure young people — women especially — into decisions not entirely their own.

Rahmani does not dismiss the concern.

"I have refused to continue a match when I sensed a woman was being pushed," he said. "Consent is not a formality in our faith. A marriage without the willing heart of both is no marriage at all. I have sent families home disappointed. I will do it again."

He acknowledges, too, that his work cannot solve the deeper anxieties driving young Iranians away from marriage. "I can introduce two good people," he said. "I cannot lower the price of an apartment."

## The Rewards of the Role

For all the complexity, Rahmani speaks most animatedly about his successes — the couples who return, sometimes with children, to thank him. He keeps their photographs in a drawer, and pulls them out with the pride of a grandfather.

"This one," he said, holding up a picture of a smiling pair, "the man was certain he would never marry. He had given up. Now look."

He estimates he has helped arrange more than 300 marriages over fifteen years. He charges modest fees, he said, and waives them entirely for those who cannot pay. The work, he insists, is a calling before it is a profession.

As afternoon light slanted through the window, another client arrived — a young engineer, nervous, clutching a folder of documents. Rahmani rose to greet him, offering tea and a place on the sofa.

"Sit, sit," the cleric said warmly. "Tell me who you are hoping to find."

Outside, the city moved on — millions of people, and among them, somewhere, perhaps a match.

---

# Love in the Time of Tradition: One Man's Quest to Modernize Iranian Matchmaking

*A story of tradition, technology, and the timeless search for connection*

---

**TEHRAN** — In a modest office tucked above a busy carpet shop in central Tehran, Reza Amini keeps a leather-bound notebook that he calls his "book of hearts." Its pages are filled with the hopes of hundreds of Iranians searching for something both simple and elusive: a life partner.

Amini, 52, has been a *khastegari* facilitator—a modern matchmaker—for nearly fifteen years. But his approach blends the deeply rooted traditions of Iranian courtship with unexpected methods that have raised eyebrows among more conservative colleagues.

"My grandmother was a matchmaker in Isfahan," Amini explains, pouring tea into small glasses etched with gold rims. "She knew every family in three villages. Today, our villages are the size of cities, and people are strangers to their own neighbors. I try to bring back what we've lost—but with the tools of today."

## A Changing Landscape

In Iran, where formal dating culture faces social and legal constraints, matchmaking retains significant cultural importance. Traditional arrangements through family networks remain common, but a new generation of educated, professional Iranians increasingly seeks alternatives.

Amini's unusual method involves what he calls "compatibility gatherings"—supervised group meetings held at his cousin's restaurant, where potential matches can converse in a respectable setting while their families wait nearby.

"The old way was two families meeting, and the young people barely speaking," he says. "But marriage is long. I believe two people should at least know if they can laugh together."

## The Hopeful Client

Among those seeking Amini's help is Maryam Hosseini, a 34-year-old pharmacist whose demanding career, she says, left little room for romance during her twenties.

"My mother worries. My aunts worry. Everyone worries but me," Maryam says with a laugh, adjusting her headscarf as she sits in Amini's waiting room. "But I decided I wanted a companion, and I wanted to be thoughtful about it. Mr. Amini takes it seriously—not just matching money to money, or family name to family name."

Maryam represents a growing demographic in urban Iran: professional women who have prioritized education and careers, sometimes finding themselves outside traditional marriage timelines.

"People assume a woman like me is too particular," she continues. "I'm not particular. I just know that I've built a life, and I want someone who respects that life, not someone who wants to erase it."

## More Than a Business

What distinguishes Amini, his clients say, is his refusal to treat matchmaking as a transaction. He interviews each client for hours, sometimes over multiple sessions, filling pages in his notebook with details about their values, their humor, their disappointments.

"I turn people away," he admits. "If someone comes to me wanting only beauty, or only wealth, I tell them to go elsewhere. I am not a merchant of people."

He has arranged, by his count, more than 200 marriages. He keeps in touch with many couples, attending the weddings of children born to matches he made a decade ago.

For Maryam, the search continues. She has met three prospective matches through Amini so far—none quite right, but each encounter respectful and, she insists, worthwhile.

"He told me something I think about often," she says. "He said, 'Finding a partner is not finding a perfect person. It is finding someone whose imperfections you can love.' For a matchmaker, he is something of a philosopher."

## Looking Forward

As evening settles over Tehran and the call to prayer echoes across the rooftops, Amini closes his book of hearts and reflects on his unusual calling.

"Young people ask me why I still do this when there are apps, when the world is changing so fast," he says. "I tell them: the world changes, but the human heart is very old. It wants the same thing it always wanted. To be known. To be chosen."

For Maryam and the hundreds of names in Amini's notebook, that ancient hope endures—carried forward, one careful introduction at a time.

---

*This is a work of fiction created for illustrative purposes. Names and specific details are invented, though they reflect broadly reported cultural dynamics around matchmaking in contemporary Iran.*

# Love in the Shadows: How Tehran's Singles Navigate the Search for Romance

**TEHRAN** — In a city where public displays of affection can draw the attention of morality police, and where dating apps exist in a legal gray zone, Iran's young singles have become masters of discretion in their pursuit of love.

Behind the modest facades of coffee shops in northern Tehran, and within the encrypted messages of smartphones, a quiet revolution in courtship is unfolding—one that blends tradition with the desires of a generation increasingly connected to the wider world.

## The Old Ways Endure

For centuries, marriage in Iran has often begun with the matchmaker, or *khastegari*, a tradition that persists even as young people seek greater autonomy.

"The families still come to me, but now the sons and daughters have their own ideas," said Mahnaz, a 58-year-old matchmaker who has arranged introductions in Tehran for over two decades and asked that only her first name be used. "Twenty years ago, a young woman would trust her parents completely. Today, she wants to meet the man three, four times. She checks his social media before she agrees to anything."

Mahnaz described her role as increasingly one of a mediator between generations. "The parents want religious, settled, from a good family. The young ones—they talk about connection, about feelings. Sometimes I feel more like a translator than a matchmaker."

## A Generation in Waiting

Iran's population skews young, and economic pressures have reshaped the timeline of adulthood. High unemployment, soaring housing costs, and inflation have pushed the average marriage age higher, leaving many in an extended period of romantic uncertainty.

Reza, a 31-year-old engineer who has been searching for a partner for several years, described the frustrations of dating in a society that offers few sanctioned venues for meeting.

"You can't just approach a woman on the street—it's not done, and it could cause problems," he said over tea in a café near Valiasr Street. "So where do you meet someone? Through friends, through family, through the apps. But the apps are complicated. You never know who is real."

Reza said economic anxiety weighs heavily on his prospects. "A woman's family will ask what I earn, whether I own an apartment. With prices the way they are, how does a young man save enough? I'm not just looking for love. I'm trying to prove I can build a life."

## The Digital Underground

Despite official restrictions, dating applications have flourished among Iran's tech-savvy youth. Some use international platforms accessed through VPNs, while a state-sanctioned matchmaking app has attempted to channel the trend into officially approved marriages.

"The young people find a way—they always find a way," Mahnaz observed with a knowing smile. "In my day, it was a note passed at a wedding. Now it's a message on the phone. The technology changes. The heart stays the same."

## Navigating Two Worlds

For many singles, daily life involves a careful negotiation between public conformity and private desire. Relationships often unfold in the homes of trusted friends, in the anonymity of the city's mountains and parks, or across the digital divide.

Reza remains hopeful, if realistic, about his chances. "My parents met through a matchmaker and they have been happy for thirty-five years," he said. "Maybe the old way, maybe the new way—I don't know which will find me my match. I just know I don't want to be alone."

As dusk settled over Tehran and the café began to fill with young patrons speaking in low tones, the search continued—quiet, persistent, and unmistakably human.

# The Matchmaker of Tehran: Inside One Mullah's Mission to Mend Iran's Marriage Crisis

*A feature profile*

---

The waiting room of the Sabz-e Zendegi Family Institute smells of cardamom tea and nervous anticipation. On a Tuesday morning in central Tehran, three couples sit on mismatched chairs, thumbing through worn copies of poetry collections while a ceiling fan turns lazily overhead. Behind a heavy wooden door, Jafar Ardabili is doing what he claims to have done more than two thousand times: talking two strangers into a lifetime together.

"Marriage," he says, adjusting the black turban that marks him as a *sayyid*, a descendant of the Prophet, "is not a contract of the head. It is a negotiation of the soul, witnessed by paperwork."

## A Different Kind of Cleric

At sixty-one, Ardabili does not fit the popular image of a stern Iranian mullah. He laughs easily, quotes the fourteenth-century poet Hafez as readily as scripture, and keeps a smartphone loaded with three separate matchmaking spreadsheets. His institute—a converted apartment near Valiasr Street—has become something of an institution in its own right over the past nineteen years.

"I began as a prayer leader," he explains, pouring tea with the deliberate care of a man performing a small ceremony. "But people kept coming to me not for God. They came for love. They came for a husband, a wife. So I thought: perhaps this, too, is God's work."

The institute occupies a peculiar niche in modern Iran, where traditional family-arranged marriages have collided with a generation that met on Instagram and dreams of self-selected romance. Ardabili positions himself squarely in that gap—part cleric, part counselor, part data-obsessed entrepreneur of the heart.

## The Numbers

By his own accounting, kept in ledgers he insists on updating by hand each evening, Ardabili has facilitated 2,340 marriages since 2005. He claims that fewer than eleven percent have ended in divorce—a figure he is quick to contrast with national statistics, which suggest that roughly one in three Iranian marriages now dissolves, and closer to one in two in Tehran itself.

"The whole country is divorcing," he says, spreading his hands in mock despair. "In my rooms, the opposite happens. I am a dam against the flood."

His method, he says, relies on what he calls the "three compatibilities": faith, family, and *khande*—laughter.

"If two people cannot laugh at the same joke," he says, "they will not survive the tax bills, the mother-in-law, the burnt rice. Anyone can love a person at a wedding. I want to know who will love them at breakfast, twenty years later, when there is no more mystery."

He charges a modest fee, he insists, and waives it entirely for the poor. "I have married the son of a carpet-seller to the daughter of a judge," he says, with evident pride. "Love does not read bank statements. Though the mothers, unfortunately, always do."

## The Waiting Room Philosophers

Among those waiting is Reza, a 29-year-old software engineer who declined to give his surname. He has visited the institute four times.

"My parents wanted the old way—a cousin, a family friend," he says quietly. "But I wanted someone who chose me, not someone chosen for me. The Hajj Agha understands both worlds. He speaks to my grandmother and to me in the same afternoon."

This dual fluency may be Ardabili's genuine gift. He can invoke the sanctity of tradition to reassure anxious parents while, in the next breath, telling a hesitant bride that she is under no obligation to marry a man she does not respect.

"I have canceled matches at the last hour," he admits. "A woman came to me weeping the night before. I told the families: better a difficult evening now than a ruined decade later. God prefers an honest cancellation to a dishonest ceremony."

## Critics and Contradictions

Not everyone celebrates the mullah of matchmaking. Some younger Iranians view the entire enterprise—clerical oversight of romance—as an anachronism, a symbol of institutions reaching into the most private corners of life. Sociologists point out that self-reported success rates from a man selling his own services deserve healthy skepticism.

Ardabili shrugs at the criticism with the ease of someone who has heard it before.

"They say I am old-fashioned," he says. "But who comes to my door? The young. The modern. The ones with the torn jeans and the foreign music in their ears. They want freedom, yes—but freedom is lonely. I offer freedom with a companion. That, they cannot download."

Pressed on whether his numbers can truly be trusted, he smiles and taps his ledger. "Come to a wedding," he says. "Count the tears of joy. That is my statistic."

## The Believer

As the interview ends, a young couple emerges from his office, shy and radiant, the particular glow of people who have just agreed to try. Ardabili rises to bless them, his turban slightly askew, his voice dropping into something gentle and almost paternal.

Later, watching them descend the stairs hand in hand, he grows briefly quiet.

"I will not live forever," he says. "But somewhere in this city, right now, there are children who exist because I sat two frightened strangers in a room and told them not to be afraid. That is a strange kind of immortality, no?"

He returns to his ledger, uncaps his pen, and begins, once more, to count.

# Seeking Love in Modern Iran: A Young Man's Journey to the Clergy

*A story of tradition and change in the Islamic Republic*

---

**TEHRAN** — On a warm afternoon in central Tehran, 27-year-old Ahmad Rezaei climbs a narrow staircase to a modest office where a cleric holds regular consultations. Ahmad, a software developer with a steady job and an easy smile, has come with a question that increasingly occupies young Iranians of his generation: how does a man find love and marriage in a country caught between religious tradition and modern longing?

"My mother wants me married," Ahmad says, adjusting his collar. "But I want to find someone I actually connect with. I don't know if those two things can happen together anymore."

## A Generation Between Worlds

Ahmad's dilemma reflects a broader tension in Iranian society. Traditional arranged introductions—known as *khastegari*, where families formally meet to discuss a potential match—remain common. Yet many young Iranians, exposed to global culture through the internet and social media, increasingly desire romantic partnerships based on personal choice.

The cleric Ahmad has come to see, Hojjat al-Islam Karimi, receives young people daily. "They come to me confused," Karimi explains, seated on a cushion beneath a portrait of religious leaders. "The old ways feel restrictive to them, but they are also afraid of the uncertainty of doing things differently."

Ahmad listens respectfully. Like many of his peers, he considers himself a believer, though his relationship with religious rules is more selective than his parents' generation.

## The Economics of Marriage

Beyond matters of the heart, Ahmad faces practical obstacles that have delayed marriage for millions of young Iranians. Economic pressures—inflation, unemployment, and a housing crisis—have made establishing a household daunting.

"The *mehriyeh* alone can be impossible," Ahmad says, referring to the mandatory dowry a groom pledges to his bride, often set in gold coins. "How can a young man promise hundreds of coins when he can barely afford rent?"

Cleric Karimi acknowledges the strain. "I tell families to be reasonable. Marriage should not become a financial prison. The Prophet, peace be upon him, favored ease in these matters." Some clergy have begun advocating for modest ceremonies and lower dowries to encourage young couples to marry.

## Technology Meets Tradition

Ahmad admits he has tried state-sanctioned matchmaking apps, which the government promotes as a wholesome alternative to Western dating platforms. These official services vet users and involve family participation, aiming to encourage marriage while discouraging casual relationships.

"It felt strange," Ahmad laughs. "Filling out forms about my religious observance and income before I even know if I like someone."

Still, he understands the appeal. In a society where unmarried men and women mixing freely can draw disapproval—or worse, attention from authorities—such platforms offer a structured path.

## The Question of Love

When Ahmad finally poses his central question—whether it is acceptable to prioritize love over family arrangement—Karimi offers a nuanced answer.

"Love is not forbidden," the cleric says. "The Quran speaks of affection and mercy between spouses. But love without wisdom, without family, without foundation—this often ends in sorrow. Seek both."

Ahmad seems partly satisfied. As he descends the stairs back into the bustling street, he reflects on the meeting. "He didn't tell me to abandon what I want," he says. "But he reminded me that I'm not just choosing for myself. That's the Iranian way, I suppose—we belong to our families."

## A Society in Transition

Ahmad's story is one among millions. Iran's marriage rate has declined in recent years while the average age of first marriage has risen, trends that worry officials who view family formation as central to the nation's religious and social fabric.

For young people like Ahmad, the path forward remains uncertain—a negotiation between faith and feeling, obligation and desire, the guidance of clerics and the pull of a changing world.

"I'll keep looking," Ahmad says, disappearing into the crowd. "And maybe I'll pray a little too. Why not use every tool available?"
